transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-06-11 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood CSM), Olivia (Hearthline CTO), Marcus (Hearthline SRE), Rita (Hearthline Product), Ben (Hearthline Legal)

Summary:
- Follow-up after last-week production cascade where a combination of batch size increase + draining timing triggered KV cache evictions causing higher latencies and some failed requests.
- Goal: agree on immediate mitigations, who owns each fallback step, and plan a canary + chaos run to validate.
- Deliverables: memory profile + trimmed benchmark, eviction traces, updated SLA/fallback ownership doc, canary schedule.

Topics covered:
- Short term containment (drain windows, sticky routing)
- Medium term: autoscale hysteresis, explicit cache pinning, limiters per-customer
- Long term: model quantization profiles and runbook for graceful degrade

Action items (read out during call): see metadata field above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Evan Brooks: hey everyone thanks for carving out time, uh, quick check — did everyone get the postmortem draft?
[00:08] Olivia Park: yes saw it, thanks. high level we appreciate the fast triage. customers were impacted for about 18 minutes, correct?
[00:15] Maya Chen: correct, the alert window was 18, with elevated tail latency after that for roughly 40 minutes while autoscale recovered.
[00:22] Marcus Lee: i pulled traces, the root was eviction oscillation in the kv cache; we saw repeated miss spikes when a few large batches hit the hot path.
[00:30] Priya Nandan: just to clarify, the runtime increased batching to improve throughput and that, combined with a slightly small mem headroom on your pool, caused continuous eviction and regen of kv entries. so every regen cost tokens and latency.
[00:44] Rita Singh: can you explain kv regen? is that cache reloading the attention kv?
[00:49] Priya Nandan: yeah, it's the kv cache for prefixes — when entries get evicted we do a warm-up on next requests which is expensive.
[00:55] Olivia Park: we had a rush of peak queries from a campaign, so the distribution shifted. our SREs didn't want to increase reserved capacity because cost tight.
[01:05] Evan Brooks: understood. the cost vs latency tradeoff comes up a lot. good news: there are targeted mitigations that don't require full capacity bump.

[01:20] Marcus Lee: quick Q: can we pin certain customer prefixes to memory so they're not evicted?
[01:25] Priya Nandan: we have a "pinning" flag in Dedicated — it can reserve cache slots per-tenant, but it needs config changes and infra permission. for hosted we can simulate via sticky routing to nodes with warmer caches.
[01:40] Olivia Park: sticky routing sounds okay but how do we make sure this doesn't create imbalance between nodes? last time one node got overloaded.
[01:48] Priya Nandan: two parts: (1) a short-term heuristic to route heavy users to a small subset of nodes with more mem headroom, with an explicit drain plan; (2) medium term, per-tenant soft limits and admission control so one tenant can't starve others.

[02:10] Evan Brooks: propose we own the routing change and provide a 48h drain window for your team to test; Redwood will instrument the nodes and provide visibility.
[02:19] Olivia Park: ok that works, who will run the drill?
[02:22] Evan Brooks: I'll coordinate, Priya will prepare the memory profile and suggested knob list.

[02:30] Marcus Lee: another ask — we want a clearer ownership matrix for fallbacks. last incident there was confusion between product and infra about who flips which fallback.
[02:37] Maya Chen: yeah, our CSM will own the operational handoff doc; we can put a runbook with step-by-step toggles. we'll also highlight which knob is safe during traffic spikes.
[02:46] Ben Koh: legal question — if Redwood flips a fallback that changes response content, do we need to pre-approve that?
[02:52] Evan Brooks: great question. fallback changes that adjust model or reduce context length can affect outputs. we can flag those as "non-breaking" vs "breaking" in the runbook; anything classified breaking requires a 30m approval window. we'll document that.

[03:10] Rita Singh: can we get timelines — short term vs medium vs long term?
[03:15] Priya Nandan: short term (days): routing heuristic + drain window + instrumentation. medium (weeks): per-tenant admission control, autoscale hysteresis tuning. long term (1-2 months): model quant profiles + pinning API for Dedicated customers.

[03:32] Marcus Lee: about the autoscale hysteresis — we saw oscillation where the cluster scaled up, then because caches were cold latency spiked and it scaled down, repeat. is that right?
[03:40] Priya Nandan: yep the feedback loop was the problem. our suggestion is adding a short cooldown and a cache-warmup policy before scaling decisions.
[03:50] Olivia Park: what about pre-warming the cache using staged replay? we can replay hot prefixes to nodes before traffic shifts.
[03:57] Priya Nandan: replay helps but it needs permissive data handling — we should ensure no sensitive PII is replayed. alternatively, seed synthetic prefixes.

[04:10] Evan Brooks: i'd like to propose the following immediate plan: (1) Redwood will push a routing change to isolate high-throughput campaign traffic to two nodes with 25% extra mem headroom for 48 hours; (2) Priya will provide mem profile and list of safe knobs; (3) Hearthline will run a staged canary with their campaign traffic on staging; (4) we run a chaos test to simulate eviction oscillation.
[04:35] Olivia Park: agree, timeline works. we need the mem profile ASAP so we can decide on reserve vs sticky.

[04:45] Ben Koh: also want the SLA language updated to call out those fallbacks and the approval windows you mentioned.
[04:51] Maya Chen: noted, i'll send the fallback ownership doc and an SLA appendix.

[05:00] Marcus Lee: small nit - can you also include a sample query rate and batch-size thresholds that you saw in the incident? that'll help recreate the load.
[05:07] Priya Nandan: yes i have the traces, i'll trim and annotate the high-water marks.

[05:15] Rita Singh: on the longer horizon, our product team is evaluating quantization to reduce mem per model. is that something Redwood supports today?
[05:22] Priya Nandan: we do — we maintain model quantization profiles and can recommend 4-bit/8-bit switches; there are quality tradeoffs so we'll attach evaluation harness results.

[05:35] Evan Brooks: ok to close the meeting, summary of next steps: Priya profile by Friday, Maya SLA doc to Ben, Marcus supply traces, schedule canary next week. we'll send calendar invites.

[05:50] Olivia Park: thanks everyone, appreciate the partnership.
[05:55] Evan Brooks: thanks, talk soon.

References mentioned during call:
